query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under mechanical loading, an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy develops stress-induced short-range chemical ordering at grain boundaries and within grains, which locally impedes dislocation motion and promotes crack nucleation, leading to brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with uniform elemental distribution and no detectable intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical loading (monotonic and cyclic) at various temperatures relevant to service conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing under both high and low temperature regimes where dislocation mobility variations are expected; loading conditions should mimic real engineering service environments to capture stress-induced microstructural evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Emergence of nanoscale, stress-induced short-range order clusters at critical regions such as grain boundaries and intragranular sites.
generation.mechanism: Applied mechanical stress amplifies local compositional fluctuations inherent to the high-entropy matrix, leading to the formation of short-range ordered regions. These regions act as barriers to dislocation movement and concentrate stress locally, thereby reducing toughness without the need for conventional, coarse intermetallic precipitates or extensive grain boundary segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogeneous baseline, mechanically loaded alloys will show increased signatures of short-range ordering (detectable by atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM), accompanied by a measurable reduction in toughness (e.g., lower fracture energy or crack initiation threshold).
generation.baseline: A uniformly structured high-entropy alloy exhibiting high toughness and ductility, with no detectable nanoscale ordering prior to mechanical intervention.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to manifest under high mechanical stress levels encountered during cyclic or high-rate loading. It may be less dominant at extreme temperatures where diffusion might rehomogenize compositions, or at very low stress levels where ordering does not trigger.
generation.uncertainty: Due to the limited direct evidence on stress-induced short-range ordering in high-entropy alloys, further detailed microstructural studies are needed to confirm this mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloy samples and subject them to identical mechanical loading protocols (monotonic and cyclic) at two temperature regimes. Monitor the microstructural evolution in situ using high-resolution TEM and post-mortem analysis via atom probe tomography to detect the formation of short-range ordered clusters. Simultaneously, measure toughness parameters (e.g., fracture toughness, crack initiation stress) before and after loading.
measurements: High-resolution imaging (TEM) to identify nanoscale ordered regions
Atom probe tomography to quantify local chemical ordering
Mechanical testing to assess changes in toughness (fracture toughness, ductility, crack propagation thresholds)
Correlative analysis between areas exhibiting SRO and crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If mechanical loading does not lead to a statistically significant increase in detectable short-range ordering or if no correlation is found between the formation of SRO and reduced toughness, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
